title: Priority-proxy + Adaptive Backoff Connector Integration Guide
author: Diego Alvarez
content:
Summary:
This guide describes recommended architecture, configuration, testing, and operational runbooks for integrating Redwood Inference with a customer or partner-side priority proxy. The pattern is intended for enterprise customers that run a multipurpose ingress layer that must: (1) prioritize latency‑sensitive inference requests, (2) handle large-volume background/async jobs without starving realtime traffic, and (3) implement an adaptive backoff strategy when Redwood responds with transient errors or capacity signals.

Goals:
- Preserve 95th/99th percentile latency SLOs for live inference routes.
- Maintain throughput for background pipelines without increasing cost to the customer.
- Provide clear telemetry and escalation hooks for degraded conditions.

Intended audience:
- Customer success engineers and integration engineers implementing ingress or API gateway policies.
- Customer platform and SRE teams responsible for on-prem or VPC deployments.

Key concepts and terminology:
- Priority Proxy: an edge or ingress proxy (e.g., Envoy, NGINX, API Gateway) that classifies and schedules requests based on route, header, or token attributes.
- Live route: low-latency user-facing inference endpoints (chat, completion, synchronously user-blocking).
- Background route: batch/async endpoints (embeddings indexing, bulk scoring) that can be queued or slowed to protect live SLOs.
- Adaptive Backoff: client-side or proxy-driven logic that reduces request rate to Redwood when observing specific signals (429s, 503s, elevated latency, or explicit capacity hints in response headers).

Architecture overview:
1) Classification: ingress annotates requests with X-Redwood-Priority: high | normal | background. Assignment should happen as early as possible (edge auth layer or API gateway).
2) Routing: priority header maps to separate internal queues/pools within the proxy. Live pool configured with fast-path (short timeouts, small queue depth). Background pool configured with large queue depth and longer retries.
3) Rate-limiting and token buckets: define separate token buckets for high and background priorities with configurable refill rates.
4) Backoff signals: Redwood will send one or more of the following signals when it detects load/capacity pressure: HTTP 429 with Retry-After, 503 Service Unavailable, X-Redwood-Capacity: degraded | constrained, and a latency-based heuristic (long tail latency > configured threshold). Proxy must translate these into adaptive backoff decisions.

Configuration reference (Envoy / Lua / NGINX examples):
- Example Envoy route filter snippet (YAML-like):

  - name: envoy.filters.http.lua
    typed_config:
      "@type": "type.googleapis.com/envoy.extensions.filters.http.lua.v3.Lua"
      inline_code: |
        function envoy_on_request(request_handle)
          local priority = request_handle:headers():get("X-Request-Priority") or "normal"
          if priority == "background" then
            request_handle:headers():add("X-Redwood-Priority", "background")
          else
            request_handle:headers():add("X-Redwood-Priority", "high")
          end
        end

- Token-bucket policy table (recommended defaults):

  | Priority  | Token refill (tokens/s) | Burst capacity (tokens) | Max queued requests |
  |-----------|-------------------------|-------------------------|---------------------|
  | high      | 100                     | 200                     | 50                  |
  | normal    | 40                      | 80                      | 200                 |
  | background| 5                       | 50                      | 1000                |

Operational backoff algorithm (recommended):
1) On first 429 or 503 for a specific backend instance: multiply current per-route request allowance by 0.6 and set a soft cooldown timer T = 10s.
2) If Retry-After present: use Retry-After as initial T (capped at 60s).
3) Exponential grow-back: every T interval without further 429/503 events, increase allowance by factor 1.25 until original baseline is reached.
4) High-priority routes are exempt from aggressive multiply unless consecutive failure rate > 10% for 30s. In that case, failover to an alternate Redwood region/model variant (see Rollout & Failover).

Example proxy policy (pseudo-config):

  policies:
    - match: {header: {X-Redwood-Priority: "high"}}
      bucket: high
      backoff_strategy: conservative
    - match: {header: {X-Redwood-Priority: "background"}}
      bucket: background
      backoff_strategy: aggressive

Integration-specific headers to surface to Redwood and to watch for in responses:
- Outbound to Redwood: X-Redwood-Priority, X-Request-Id, X-Customer-Tenant, X-Client-Version
- Expected Redwood response headers: Retry-After, X-Redwood-Capacity, X-Redwood-Model-Variant

Telemetry and dashboards (minimum required):
- Per-priority request rate (RPS) and error rate (4xx/5xx)
- 95th/99th latency by priority and route
- 429/503 count and Retry-After distribution
- Queue depth per pool and token-bucket token consumption
- Model variant fallback counts and failover reasons

Suggested Grafana panels and alerts:
- Alert: High-priority 99p latency > 800ms for 5m -> Sev 2, notify customer SRE and CSM.
- Alert: High-priority error rate > 5% for 3m -> Sev 1, trigger incident process.
- Alert: Background queue depth > 75% capacity for 10m -> Pager to integration owner (warn).
- Alert: Adaptive backoff active for > 2 min and RPS still > 50% of baseline -> Ops review.

Testing and validation checklist (pre-go-live):
1) Functional test: verify X-Redwood-Priority header set correctly for all client types.
2) Failure simulation: Return 429 and 503 from a Redwood test backend and verify proxy reduces allowance per algorithm and that Retry-After is respected.
3) Load test: Run mixed workload that mirrors production split (example: 70% background, 30% live) and confirm high route p95/p99 latency remains within SLO at target baseline.
4) Chaos test: introduce model-variant failover and confirm client receives X-Redwood-Model-Variant header and traffic migrates per routing policy.
5) Telemetry validation: Ensure metrics show expected buckets and queue depth; test alert firing thresholds in staging.

Rollout and fallback steps:
1) Canary: Enable policies for 5% of traffic (by IP range or customer id). Monitor latency and error metrics for 30 minutes.
2) Ramp: 20% -> 50% -> 100% over incremental windows no shorter than 30 minutes after no alerts.
3) On alert (see conditions above): revert to previous proxy policy snapshot and open a ticket with Redwood CS with attached telemetry.
4) If Redwood signals capacity degraded for single region/model variant, initiate automatic failover to configured secondary region/model variant and notify stakeholders.

Operational runbook (play-by-play):
1) Detection: Alert fires for high-priority p99 latency.
2) Triage: On-call runs the following checks: per-route p99, queue depth, 429/503 spike, any active adaptive-backoff windows.
3) Short-term mitigation: Increase high-priority token refill by 10% (if safe), drain background tokens by 30%, and increase replica count for client-side frontends if autoscaling available.
4) Escalation: If mitigation fails within 10 minutes and error rates remain high, escalate to Redwood Customer Success and Eng SRE. Include: last 15m traces, p95/p99 history, and recent model variant headers.
5) Post-incident: Run RCA within 72 hours and update proxy policy with tuned thresholds.

Escalation contacts and ownership:
- Customer oncall/SRE: provided by customer (document here).
- Redwood CSM: Diego Alvarez (d.alvarez@redwood.example.com)
- Redwood Eng SRE escalation: eng-sre-oncall@redwood.example.com
- Priority escalation steps: open ticket at support.redwood.example.com -> tag as "priority-proxy" -> page oncall and CSM.

Common pitfalls and mitigations:
- Pitfall: Over-aggressive background throttling starves pipelines for hours.
  Mitigation: implement slow-fail queue drains with observable cutoff metrics and secondary offload to batch worker pool.
- Pitfall: Missing X-Request-Id header prevents tracing across systems.
  Mitigation: fail early and add generated request id at ingress if client absent.
- Pitfall: Relying only on latency heuristics can produce false positives under GC or networking blips.
  Mitigation: combine latency signal with 429/503 counts and Retry-After presence.

Appendix A — Example cURL smoke test:

  curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $REDWOOD_KEY" -H "X-Redwood-Priority: high" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"input": "hello"}' https://api.redwood.example.com/v1/generate

Expected successful response headers:
- X-Redwood-Model-Variant: gptx-1.2
- X-Redwood-Capacity: available

Appendix B — Minimal policy JSON (example for integration with managed gateway):

  {"policies": [{"match": {"header": {"X-Redwood-Priority": "high"}}, "bucket": "high", "max_inflight": 50, "backoff": {"multiplier": 0.6, "cooldown_sec": 10}}, {"match": {"header": {"X-Redwood-Priority": "background"}}, "bucket": "background", "max_inflight": 1000, "backoff": {"multiplier": 0.25, "cooldown_sec": 30}}]}

Appendix C — Onboarding checklist (CS-led activities):
- Confirm ingress header mapping and token-bucket defaults.
- Run the testing and validation checklist with CSM present.
- Schedule QBR telemetries: include per-priority latency panels and adaptation history.
- Agree on escalation playbook and contact list.
